lessons.title: Agile Foundations: Responding to Change
lessons.purpose: In this lesson, you will learn what Agile is and why teams use it. You will examine the four Agile Manifesto values. You will compare Agile and predictive ways of responding to change. You will also explain how short cycles, feedback, and small product increments can lower risk.

student_hub.title: Join the Student Hub product team
student_hub.alt: A smartphone displaying a calendar style app icon with a checkmark and event markers.
student_hub.caption: Student Hub is the app your team will improve throughout this module.
body: Student Hub is a work in progress app for assignments, deadlines, and course events. You are joining the product team.
Across eight lessons, you will help guide each update. You will listen to users, organize work, test ideas, and improve the app as new evidence appears.
As you compare choices, use evidence, product value, and risk to justify why a small tested increment should come before less urgent work.

Your explanation should connect the evidence to an Agile value, identify the risk in the original plan, and describe how a limited experiment produces information before the team commits more development time.
This kind of justification is important in software work because teams often balance user access, stakeholder value, technical uncertainty, and limited capacity at the same time.
student_hub.challenge: The team planned to build event reminders next. New tests reveal problems with phone and keyboard access. Your first task is to help the team decide what to do next.
bullets: Study what users and tests reveal.
Use Agile ideas to choose the team's next work.
Recommend a small product change the team can test.

objectives: L1 O1 Explain how Agile values guide decisions when needs change.
L1 O2 Compare Agile and predictive responses to changing user needs.
L1 O3 Explain how short cycles, feedback, and small product increments reduce risk.

vocabulary.definition: A way of developing software in short cycles so a team can learn from feedback and adapt.
A development approach that relies on a detailed plan made early in the project.
Repeated in short cycles so the team can learn and improve.
Built in small usable pieces instead of all at once.
Information from users, stakeholders, tests, or team members that helps improve the product or process.

2.title: Connect and Learn: When Plans Change
2.focus: Think of a time when new information changed a plan. What changed? What did you do next? Keep your answer in mind.
body: LEARN, Software teams do not know every detail at the start. Agile helps them learn while they build. In each short cycle, a team plans, builds, tests, and gets feedback. Then the team uses that evidence to improve the product.
A predictive approach creates a detailed plan early and generally follows that plan unless it is formally changed. An Agile approach uses new evidence to adjust what the team does next.

One cycle is called an iteration. A usable piece of the product is an increment. Feedback can come from users, stakeholders, tests, or teammates. Agile teams still plan, record key choices, and protect quality. They change the plan when evidence points to a better path.

graphic.alt: Five stage iterative cycle with a usable Increment at the center and an arrow from improvement back to planning.
graphic.caption: Short cycles help a software team plan, build, test, gather feedback, and improve.

Stop planning and react to every request.

check.feedback_correct: Correct. Agile teams use evidence to update plans while protecting quality.
check.feedback_incorrect: Review how feedback helps a team change its plan without giving up planning or quality.

after_graphic: Now connect the cycle to Student Hub. Students report that the calendar does not work well on a phone. The team can study that feedback and plan a small fix. This choice protects quality and responds to a real user need.

lessons.title: Scrum and the Agile Team
lessons.purpose: In this lesson, you will learn what Scrum is. Scrum helps one Agile team work in short cycles. You will identify the Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers, and stakeholders. You will also explain how a cross functional, self managing team works together.

vocabulary.definition: An Agile framework teams can use to build and improve a product in short cycles.

2.title: Connect and Learn: What Is Scrum?
2.focus: Work on your own. Think about a team that has to build something useful in a short time. What would help the team stay focused? Keep one idea in mind.
body: LEARN, Scrum is one Agile framework. A framework is a simple structure a team can use to organize work. Scrum does not replace Agile values. It gives the team clear roles, events, and artifacts. These parts help the team see the work.

A Scrum Team works toward one Product Goal. The team plans a short cycle of work. It creates a usable product Increment. Then the team inspects feedback and adapts what comes next. Scrum helps Student Hub stay focused as needs change.

3.title: Scrum Team Accountabilities
3.focus: Watch for how each Scrum role helps the Student Hub team make a different decision.
body: A Scrum Team has three accountabilities. An accountability is an area of responsibility. It is not a job rank. The three accountabilities are Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers.
The Product Owner is accountable for product value and Product Backlog order. This person decides which outcomes and backlog items matter most.
Developers create each usable Increment. They decide how to organize, build, and test the selected work.
The Scrum Master helps the team understand and use Scrum well. This person coaches the team and helps the team address barriers.
Stakeholders are not members of the Scrum Team. They share needs, evidence, and feedback. For Student Hub, stakeholders may include students, teachers, families, office staff, or support staff.

4.title: Cross Functional and Self Organizing Teams
4.focus: Watch for why a Scrum Team needs different skills and why Developers help organize their own work.
body: A cross functional team has the skills needed to create a usable product Increment. The team may need coding, design, testing, data, security, accessibility, and communication skills. Not every person needs every skill. The team needs enough skills across the group.

A self managing team decides how to organize its work. Developers do not wait for a boss to assign every task. They plan together, make work visible, ask for help, and adjust the plan when they learn more.

For Student Hub, the team may need one person to improve the calendar layout, another to test keyboard access, and another to check account data. The team works together around one goal instead of handing work from one silo to another.

A short description of a user’s need, goal, and reason for wanting a feature.

2.title: Connect and Learn: User Stories
2.focus: Work on your own. A student says, “I miss assignments because the Student Hub list is hard to scan on my phone.” What does the team need to know before building? Keep two questions in mind.
body: LEARN, User needs often begin as broad requests. A software team needs to clarify the need before it builds. A user story is one common Agile practice. It is not an official Scrum artifact.
A common format is: As a [user], I want [goal], so that [benefit]. The user tells who needs the feature. The goal states what the person needs. The benefit explains why it matters.
A strong user story focuses on value. It does not force one solution too early. For Student Hub, the team should understand the student’s problem before choosing a design or code change.

3.title: Acceptance Criteria Make Work Testable
3.focus: Watch for how acceptance criteria help a team decide whether a story is ready to build and complete.
body: Acceptance criteria describe what must be true for a story to work. Each criterion should be observable and testable. A tester should be able to check it without guessing.
Criteria describe product results, not development tasks. “Build the filter quickly” is not testable enough. “Keyboard users can reach and use the date filter” is testable because someone can try it.
Acceptance criteria also help the team protect access and quality. For Student Hub, the team can include criteria for small screens, keyboard use, clear messages, and correct results.
The Product Backlog may contain user stories, but Scrum does not require that format. Developers use clear backlog items and the Definition of Done to create a usable Increment.
Professional teams avoid vague backlog work because vague work creates rework, missed expectations, and testing confusion.
Acceptance criteria should describe observable behavior, conditions, and results so the team can inspect the Increment against shared evidence.

lessons.title: Prioritize the Student Hub Backlog
lessons.purpose: In this lesson, you will help the Student Hub team decide what work should come first. You will use a Product Backlog to make work visible and use evidence about value, risk, need, and effort to explain the order.
objectives: L4 O1 Explain how a Product Backlog supports transparent product decisions.
L4 O2 Order backlog items using stakeholder evidence, value, risk, need, and effort.

vocabulary.definition: An ordered list of work needed to improve the product.
One piece of work in the Product Backlog, such as a feature, fix, or research task.
Ongoing work to make backlog items clearer, smaller, and ready for future planning.
The relative importance or order of work.
The benefit a product or feature gives to users, stakeholders, or the team.
Something that could cause harm, delay, confusion, or poor quality if not handled.

2.title: Connect and Learn: One Backlog, Changing Order
2.focus: Work on your own. The Student Hub team can complete only two of five requests. What facts would you want before choosing? Keep two kinds of evidence in mind.
body: A Product Backlog is an ordered list of work needed to improve a product. It is the single source of work for the Scrum Team.

Backlog items may describe features, fixes, research, or other needs. The Product Owner is accountable for Product Backlog management. This includes making items clear and ordering them to improve product value.
An ordered backlog is not a fixed promise. The team changes it as users give feedback and new risks appear. Teams may consider user value, urgency, risk, evidence, need, and effort.
For example, an access barrier may move above a color theme request because it blocks students from using the product. Effort matters, but the smallest item is not always the most valuable.

3.title: Prioritization and Visible Work
3.focus: As you watch and read, look for how cards and columns help a team see what work is ready, active, blocked, or done.
body: A team can use a simple board to make work visible. A priority board can show what is Ready, Next, or Later. A workflow board can show what is Ready, In Progress, Blocked, or Done.
The board helps people see the current order and discuss changes. It does not choose priorities for the team.
The Product Owner remains accountable for Product Backlog ordering. Kanban style boards are common Agile tools, but they are not required Scrum artifacts.

A minimum viable product, or MVP, is the smallest usable version of a product that can provide value and support learning. MVP is a common product planning term, not a required Scrum artifact. An MVP should still meet quality and access needs.

When evidence conflicts, ask which item creates the most value or reduces the greatest risk. Also consider who is affected and how strong the evidence is. Record a short reason for each high priority item so the decision can be reviewed later.

2.title: Connect and Learn: What Is Sprint Planning?
2.focus: Work on your own. In Lesson 4, the Student Hub team ordered the Product Backlog. Now the team has 13 capacity points and 26 points of possible work. What should the team decide before selecting items? Keep value and capacity in mind.
body: Sprint Planning starts the Sprint by helping the Scrum Team decide why the Sprint is valuable.
That purpose becomes the Sprint Goal. A good Sprint Goal gives the team one shared outcome instead of a loose list of tasks.
The team also looks at the ordered Product Backlog, available capacity, past results, and quality expectations before it selects work.
Capacity means the amount of work the team can realistically handle during the Sprint. The team should not fill every available point. A small buffer helps it respond to normal uncertainty.

lessons.title: Daily Scrum, Teamwork, and Blockers
lessons.purpose: In this lesson, you will learn how the Daily Scrum helps Developers inspect progress and adapt the plan. You will also learn why some workplaces call a short team check in a daily stand up. You will identify blockers, spot work that puts the Sprint Goal at risk, and choose next actions that help the team adjust.
objectives: L6 O1 Explain how the Daily Scrum helps Developers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal.
L6 O2 Identify blockers, impediments, and Sprint Goal risks from team updates.
L6 O3 Choose next actions that adapt the Sprint Backlog while preserving team self management.

vocabulary.definition: A short Scrum event where Developers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt their plan.

2.title: Connect and Learn: What Is the Daily Scrum?
2.focus: Work on your own. In Lesson 5, the Student Hub team planned a Sprint. Now work has started. A teammate says, "I am still working on it." What details would help the team decide what to do next? Keep two details in mind.
body: The Daily Scrum is a 15 minute event for the Developers. Its purpose is to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog.
The Daily Scrum is not a status report to a manager. Developers use it to plan the next workday. They choose the format that helps them inspect progress and make a useful adjustment.
A strong Daily Scrum update connects work to the Sprint Goal, names evidence, and makes a blocker clear. A blocker is anything that slows or stops needed work.

3.title: Daily Stand Ups in the Workplace
3.focus: Watch for how short team check ins make work visible. Notice the connection between a stand up, a Daily Scrum, and the team's plan for the next workday.
body: Many workplaces use the phrase daily stand up for a short team check in. In Scrum, the event is called the Daily Scrum. The Scrum name matters because it has a clear purpose: Developers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt their plan.

This distinction helps the team avoid a common mistake. The event is not a full status meeting, a long problem solving session, or a report to a boss. It is most useful when team members share the information needed to keep important, time sensitive work moving.

When a team practices self management, Developers organize their own work instead of waiting for one person to assign every task. A clear stand up update gives the team enough information to choose a responsible next action.

4.title: Progress, Blockers, and Adaptation
4.focus: Watch for the difference between a blocker the team can handle and an impediment that needs help from someone outside the team.
body: A blocker is a problem that stops or slows needed work. Some blockers can be handled by the Developers. For example, Developers might pair on difficult work, ask for needed information, or reorder tasks in the Sprint Backlog.

An impediment is a barrier that the Scrum Team cannot remove on its own. The Scrum Master helps when the problem is outside the team's authority or ability. The Scrum Master supports the team, but does not assign the Developers' work.

Transparency means making important work and problems visible. Inspection means reviewing the current evidence. Adaptation means changing the plan when the evidence shows a need. During or after the Daily Scrum, Developers may update the Sprint Backlog so the plan still protects the Sprint Goal.

Some problems need a longer discussion after the Daily Scrum. The team should keep the event focused, record a clear next action, and involve the people who can help. This keeps the Daily Scrum useful while giving larger problems the time and attention they deserve.

The important decision is not who sounds busiest. The important decision is whether the current evidence changes the team's plan. When Developers name a blocker, explain its impact, and choose a specific follow up, they protect the Sprint Goal without turning the Daily Scrum into a lecture or a manager led status meeting.

check.feedback_correct: Correct. The team makes the impediment visible and gets help without giving up self management.
check.feedback_incorrect: Ask whether the team can solve the blocker itself or needs help outside the team.

lessons.title: Review, Feedback, and Continuous Improvement
lessons.purpose: In this lesson, you will use Sprint Review feedback to improve the product and retrospective evidence to improve the team's process. You will keep product feedback and process feedback separate so each one leads to the right next action.

2.title: Connect and Learn: Sprint Review Feedback
2.focus: Work on your own. The Student Hub team demonstrates a feature that works, but users find a serious problem. What should the team do with that feedback? Keep one next action in mind.
body: LEARN, The Sprint Review is a Scrum event for inspecting the product result. The Scrum Team and stakeholders look at what was built, what changed, and what should happen next.
The Sprint Review is not only a presentation. It is a working session. Stakeholder feedback may lead the Product Owner to reorder the Product Backlog.

For Student Hub, students may report that search works but the results are hard to scan on a phone. The team should not promise every request. It should compare the feedback with product value, risk, and the Product Goal.
Product feedback answers this question: What did we learn about the product or the people who use it?

2.title: Connect and Learn: One Scrum Informed Agile Cycle
2.focus: Work on your own. Think through this order: gather user evidence, plan a Sprint, build and test an Increment, review feedback, and improve the process. Keep one connection in mind as you continue.
body: LEARN, This Scrum informed cycle shows one way Agile teams connect important decisions across a project. Teams adapt their practices as needs, constraints, and evidence change.
A user need helps the team shape a Product Goal. The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog using value, risk, evidence, and effort.
During Sprint Planning, the Scrum Team creates a Sprint Goal. Developers select work that supports the goal and create a Sprint Backlog.

During the Sprint, Developers inspect progress and adapt their plan. At the Sprint Review, the team and stakeholders inspect the product result. At the Sprint Retrospective, the team chooses one way to improve how it works.
Agile teams still plan. They use repeated planning, working results, and feedback to reduce risk.

3.title: Agile Toolkit and Definition of Done
3.focus: Watch for how Scrum artifacts connect to goals and quality. Then focus on why working is not the same as done.
body: Use this toolkit when a software project changes. Product Goal describes the future value the product should create. Product Backlog is the ordered list of possible product work. Sprint Goal states the value or purpose for the current Sprint. Sprint Backlog shows the selected work and the Developers' plan.

Scrum artifacts have commitments. The Product Backlog connects to the Product Goal. The Sprint Backlog connects to the Sprint Goal. The Increment connects to the Definition of Done. These links help the team make work and quality visible.
A usable Increment is completed product work that can provide value. In Scrum, work becomes part of an Increment only when it meets the Definition of Done.
The Definition of Done is the team's shared quality standard. It helps the team avoid calling work complete before testing, access, and other required quality checks are finished.
This matters in the final Student Hub challenge. A reminder feature may look like it works, but it is not done if keyboard users cannot set or cancel reminders as required by the acceptance criteria.

assessment_bank.prompt: A client changes an important need after development begins. Which action best follows Agile practice?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Agile teams use new evidence to adjust future work.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Choose the action that combines feedback, planning, and quality.
assessment_bank.option_a: Ignore the need until the original work is complete.
assessment_bank.option_b: Review the evidence and adjust future work while protecting quality.
assessment_bank.option_c: Replace all team processes with informal talks.
assessment_bank.option_d: Promise the change without checking its effect on other work.

assessment_bank.prompt: Which statement best compares Agile and predictive development?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Agile uses repeated cycles to inspect work and make changes.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Both approaches can use plans and documents. Focus on how each responds to feedback and change.
assessment_bank.option_a: Agile avoids plans, but predictive development requires them.
assessment_bank.option_b: Agile uses repeated feedback. Predictive work relies more on an early sequence.
assessment_bank.option_c: Agile removes documents. Predictive development records every decision.
assessment_bank.option_d: Agile is only for small products. Predictive work is only for large products.

assessment_bank.prompt: The Student Hub team builds a usable calendar view. Students test it, and the team improves it in the next cycle. What does this show?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The team builds a usable improvement and learns during another cycle.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Look for repeated cycles and a usable product improvement.
assessment_bank.option_a: One predictive phase
assessment_bank.option_b: An iterative and incremental approach
assessment_bank.option_c: A project without requirements
assessment_bank.option_d: A release without quality checks

assessment_bank.prompt: A team values responding to change over following a plan. What does this mean?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The plan matters, but evidence may support a change.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: The Agile values do not say that the item on the right has no value.
assessment_bank.option_a: Plans have no value after work begins.
assessment_bank.option_b: Every new request must enter the current Sprint.
assessment_bank.option_c: The team may update its plan when evidence shows a better path.
assessment_bank.option_d: The team should wait for complete certainty before planning.

assessment_bank.prompt: Which Student Hub action gives the best evidence of customer collaboration?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Students inspect working software, and their feedback guides the next decision.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Customer collaboration means that user input helps shape the product.
assessment_bank.option_a: Choose features only by coding time.
assessment_bank.option_b: Ask students to test a calendar increment and use their feedback.
assessment_bank.option_c: Follow the first feature list without meeting users again.
assessment_bank.option_d: Wait until the whole product is done before showing it.

assessment_bank.prompt: Who is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog to maximize product value?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The Product Owner is accountable for Product Backlog management and maximizing value.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Separate decisions about what matters most from decisions about how Developers complete the work.
assessment_bank.option_a: The Product Owner
assessment_bank.option_b: The Scrum Master
assessment_bank.option_c: The Developers
assessment_bank.option_d: The stakeholders

assessment_bank.prompt: The Student Hub Developers disagree about how to test a feature. What is the best Scrum aligned response?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Developers decide how to organize and complete their work.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: A self managing Scrum Team does not depend on a Scrum Master or Product Owner to assign Developers' tasks.
assessment_bank.option_a: Ask the Scrum Master to assign the testing method.
assessment_bank.option_b: Let the Developers discuss the evidence and organize the work themselves.
assessment_bank.option_c: Ask stakeholders to divide the team's tasks.
assessment_bank.option_d: Have the Product Owner select each testing task.

assessment_bank.prompt: Which action best represents the Scrum Master's accountability?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The Scrum Master helps establish Scrum and improve team effectiveness.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: The Scrum Master supports the team and Scrum practice but is not the team's manager.
assessment_bank.option_a: Choosing which feature has the highest product value
assessment_bank.option_b: Coaching the team to use Scrum effectively and address barriers
assessment_bank.option_c: Approving every technical decision before work begins
assessment_bank.option_d: Writing all Product Backlog items for the Product Owner

assessment_bank.prompt: A group of students tests a Student Hub Increment and reports that navigation is confusing. What role are the students serving?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Stakeholders provide needs, evidence, and feedback about the product.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: The three Scrum Team accountabilities are Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers. Other people who provide product feedback are stakeholders.
assessment_bank.option_a: Developers
assessment_bank.option_b: Product Owners
assessment_bank.option_c: Stakeholders
assessment_bank.option_d: Scrum Masters

assessment_bank.prompt: Which team behavior gives the strongest evidence of self management?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. A self managing team decides internally who does what, when, and how.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Look for a response in which team members organize their own work while staying focused on the shared goal.
assessment_bank.option_a: One person assigns every task and approves every decision.
assessment_bank.option_b: Team members wait for stakeholders to solve an internal blocker.
assessment_bank.option_c: Developers inspect progress, divide work, and adjust their plan together.
assessment_bank.option_d: The Scrum Master completes blocked tasks for the Developers.

assessment_bank.prompt: Which user story includes a user, goal, and benefit?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The story names the user, goal, and benefit.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Look for who needs something, what the person needs, and why it matters.
assessment_bank.option_a: Add a better assignment list.
assessment_bank.option_b: As a student, I want to sort assignments by due date so that I can plan my week.
assessment_bank.option_c: The team should create a sort button.
assessment_bank.option_d: Students need an improved page.

assessment_bank.prompt: Why should a user story focus on value instead of one technical solution?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The story describes the need while Developers decide how to build it.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: A user story should make the need clear without deciding every technical detail.
assessment_bank.option_a: It gives Developers room to choose an effective solution.
assessment_bank.option_b: It prevents stakeholders from sharing feedback.
assessment_bank.option_c: It removes the need for acceptance criteria.
assessment_bank.option_d: It guarantees that the story will fit in one Sprint.

assessment_bank.prompt: Which statement is a testable acceptance criterion?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. A tester can measure the loading time on the named device.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Choose a product result that can be observed or measured.
assessment_bank.option_a: The page should feel simple.
assessment_bank.option_b: The feature should be popular.
assessment_bank.option_c: The assignment list loads in five seconds or less on the test device.
assessment_bank.option_d: The Developers should write clean code.

assessment_bank.prompt: A Student Hub story says, “As a teacher, I want to post an announcement so that students see urgent news.” What should the team add next?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Acceptance criteria define the results needed for the story to work.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: The story explains the need and value. The team still needs clear conditions for success.
assessment_bank.option_a: A list of unrelated features
assessment_bank.option_b: Testable acceptance criteria
assessment_bank.option_c: A new Product Goal
assessment_bank.option_d: The name of one assigned Developer

assessment_bank.prompt: Which statement about user stories is accurate?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Teams may use user stories, but they are not required Scrum artifacts.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Separate common Agile practices from the required parts of Scrum.
assessment_bank.option_a: Scrum requires every Product Backlog item to use a user story.
assessment_bank.option_b: A user story is a common Agile practice, but Scrum does not require it.
assessment_bank.option_c: Only the Scrum Master may write a user story.
assessment_bank.option_d: A user story replaces all product testing.

assessment_bank.prompt: What is a Product Backlog?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The Product Backlog is an ordered list of work needed to improve the product.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: The backlog shows possible future product work and changes as the team learns.
assessment_bank.option_a: A fixed list that cannot change
assessment_bank.option_b: An ordered list of work needed to improve a product
assessment_bank.option_c: A list of tasks assigned only by the Scrum Master
assessment_bank.option_d: A record of work already completed

assessment_bank.prompt: Which evidence gives the strongest reason to move a backlog item higher?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Evidence that users are blocked shows high need and risk.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Use evidence about product value, access, need, and risk instead of personal preference.
assessment_bank.option_a: One team member likes the idea.
assessment_bank.option_b: The item has the shortest title.
assessment_bank.option_c: Testing shows that the current feature blocks keyboard users.
assessment_bank.option_d: The item was added to the backlog first.

assessment_bank.prompt: Who is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The Product Owner is accountable for Product Backlog management and ordering.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Stakeholders and Developers may provide evidence, but the Product Owner remains accountable for the order.
assessment_bank.option_a: The Product Owner
assessment_bank.option_b: The Scrum Master
assessment_bank.option_c: The Developers
assessment_bank.option_d: All stakeholders by vote

assessment_bank.prompt: What does a simple Agile board help a team do?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. A board makes work and its current status easier to see.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: The board displays work. It does not guarantee results or prevent changes.
assessment_bank.option_a: Guarantee that every item will be finished
assessment_bank.option_b: Make work and its status visible
assessment_bank.option_c: Replace feedback from users
assessment_bank.option_d: Prevent the backlog from changing

assessment_bank.prompt: The team receives reliable new user evidence. What should happen next?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The backlog should change when new evidence supports a better order.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: An ordered backlog guides current decisions, but it is not a fixed promise.
assessment_bank.option_a: Keep the old order so the plan stays stable.
assessment_bank.option_b: Review the backlog order and change it when the evidence supports a better choice.
assessment_bank.option_c: Delete every low priority item.
assessment_bank.option_d: Start all backlog items at the same time.

assessment_bank.prompt: What is the main purpose of a Sprint Goal?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The Sprint Goal states why the Sprint is valuable.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: The goal guides the Sprint without fixing every task.
assessment_bank.option_a: Give the Sprint one shared purpose
assessment_bank.option_b: Assign every task to one person
assessment_bank.option_c: Prevent all changes to the plan
assessment_bank.option_d: List every future product feature

assessment_bank.prompt: What should Developers consider when selecting Sprint work?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. A realistic plan connects value with capacity and quality.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Select work the team can finish to the Definition of Done.
assessment_bank.option_a: Only how interesting each item seems
assessment_bank.option_b: Priority, capacity, dependencies, and quality
assessment_bank.option_c: The number of people watching the project
assessment_bank.option_d: Whether every backlog item can fit

assessment_bank.prompt: Who owns the detailed plan in the Sprint Backlog?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Developers create and update their plan.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: The Product Owner orders product work, while Developers plan how to complete selected work.
assessment_bank.option_a: Stakeholders
assessment_bank.option_b: The Scrum Master
assessment_bank.option_c: The Developers
assessment_bank.option_d: An outside manager

assessment_bank.prompt: When is work part of a usable Increment?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Work must meet the Definition of Done to be part of the Increment.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Selected or started work is not complete until it meets the agreed quality level.
assessment_bank.option_a: When coding begins
assessment_bank.option_b: When a stakeholder requests it
assessment_bank.option_c: When it meets the Definition of Done
assessment_bank.option_d: When it enters the Sprint Backlog

assessment_bank.prompt: Developers learn that a task is larger than expected. What is the best response?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Developers adapt the plan as they learn while staying focused on the goal.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: The Sprint Backlog is an evolving plan, not a fixed promise.
assessment_bank.option_a: Update the Sprint Backlog and protect the Sprint Goal.
assessment_bank.option_b: Keep the old plan even when it no longer works.
assessment_bank.option_c: Lower quality so every task fits.
assessment_bank.option_d: Add more unrelated work.

assessment_bank.prompt: What is the purpose of the Daily Scrum?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Developers inspect progress and adapt the Sprint Backlog.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: The event helps Developers plan their work, not report to a manager.
assessment_bank.option_a: Report status to a manager
assessment_bank.option_b: Inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan
assessment_bank.option_c: Solve every technical problem
assessment_bank.option_d: Approve the Product Backlog

assessment_bank.prompt: Who is the Daily Scrum for?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The Daily Scrum is an event for Developers.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Other people may attend in limited cases, but Developers conduct the event.
assessment_bank.option_a: Developers
assessment_bank.option_b: Only the Product Owner
assessment_bank.option_c: Only stakeholders
assessment_bank.option_d: An outside manager

assessment_bank.prompt: Which action shows adaptation after a blocker appears?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The team uses evidence to update its plan.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Adaptation changes the plan when current evidence shows a need.
assessment_bank.option_a: Hide the blocker
assessment_bank.option_b: Update the Sprint Backlog and agree on a next action
assessment_bank.option_c: Keep every task in the same order
assessment_bank.option_d: Wait until the Sprint ends

assessment_bank.prompt: What should a Scrum Master do when an impediment affects the team?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The Scrum Master helps the team address impediments and improve effectiveness.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: The Scrum Master supports the team but does not become its boss.
assessment_bank.option_a: Assign every Developer a new task
assessment_bank.option_b: Help the team address the impediment while supporting self management
assessment_bank.option_c: Cancel the Sprint without the Product Owner
assessment_bank.option_d: Take over the blocked work

assessment_bank.prompt: Which Daily Scrum behavior best protects the Sprint Goal?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Specific evidence and next actions help Developers protect the goal.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Useful communication supports inspection, adaptation, and self management.
assessment_bank.option_a: Give vague updates so the event stays short
assessment_bank.option_b: Discuss evidence, blockers, and the next useful action
assessment_bank.option_c: Add unrelated work whenever someone has time
assessment_bank.option_d: Wait for one person to assign all work

assessment_bank.prompt: What does a Sprint Review inspect?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The review examines the outcome and what to do next.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Focus on the product, stakeholders, and future decisions.
assessment_bank.option_a: The product outcome and possible future work
assessment_bank.option_b: Only individual performance
assessment_bank.option_c: Only the team's meeting rules
assessment_bank.option_d: A final plan that cannot change

assessment_bank.prompt: Stakeholders report a new access problem. What should the team do?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Feedback can guide Product Backlog adaptation.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: The team considers the evidence without promising every request.
assessment_bank.option_a: Ignore it until the product is finished
assessment_bank.option_b: Use the evidence to reconsider future Product Backlog work
assessment_bank.option_c: Add it to the current Sprint without discussion
assessment_bank.option_d: Cancel every planned feature

assessment_bank.prompt: What is the main focus of a Sprint Retrospective?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The retrospective plans improvements to how the team works.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Separate process improvement from product inspection.
assessment_bank.option_a: Improving team quality and effectiveness
assessment_bank.option_b: Demonstrating the Increment to stakeholders
assessment_bank.option_c: Ordering the Product Backlog
assessment_bank.option_d: Selecting a new Product Goal

assessment_bank.prompt: Which action is a useful retrospective improvement?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The action is specific and testable.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: A useful improvement names a behavior the team can try.
assessment_bank.option_a: Work faster.
assessment_bank.option_b: Never make mistakes.
assessment_bank.option_c: Check access criteria together before development begins.
assessment_bank.option_d: Remove all testing from the Sprint.

assessment_bank.prompt: Which statement correctly separates the two events?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The events inspect different evidence and support different changes.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Review the product in the Sprint Review and the team's process in the retrospective.
assessment_bank.option_a: The Sprint Review improves the product plan; the retrospective improves the team's process.
assessment_bank.option_b: Both events only inspect individual performance.
assessment_bank.option_c: The review changes team habits; the retrospective gathers user needs.
assessment_bank.option_d: Both events create a fixed plan.

assessment_bank.prompt: Which action best reflects Agile values?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Agile teams share useful work, gather evidence, and adapt.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Look for working results, collaboration, and response to change.
assessment_bank.option_a: Follow the first plan even when evidence changes
assessment_bank.option_b: Share working software and use feedback to adapt
assessment_bank.option_c: Delay user input until the entire product is complete
assessment_bank.option_d: Replace team communication with detailed tools

assessment_bank.prompt: When is a predictive approach different from an Agile approach?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Predictive work depends more on an early plan and sequence.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Focus on how each approach responds to new evidence.
assessment_bank.option_a: It uses quality standards
assessment_bank.option_b: It assigns work to a team
assessment_bank.option_c: It includes a product goal
assessment_bank.option_d: It relies more on an early sequence and limits later change

assessment_bank.prompt: Why do teams develop software in short cycles?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Short cycles create repeated chances to learn and improve.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Choose the answer that connects working software with evidence.
assessment_bank.option_a: They can test useful work, gather feedback, and improve it
assessment_bank.option_b: They can avoid planning and documentation
assessment_bank.option_c: They can complete every feature at the same time
assessment_bank.option_d: They can prevent stakeholders from changing priorities

assessment_bank.prompt: Testing reveals that keyboard users cannot use a new feature. What should the team do next?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Iterative development uses test evidence to improve the product.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Use the failed test as evidence for the next action.
assessment_bank.option_a: Release it because the Sprint has ended
assessment_bank.option_b: Remove accessibility from the Definition of Done
assessment_bank.option_c: Use the result to revise and retest the Increment
assessment_bank.option_d: Wait until the full product is complete

assessment_bank.prompt: A stakeholder asks for a Student Hub feature, but the request is too broad to build. What should the team do first?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Strong backlog items and user stories turn broad needs into clear, testable work.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Look for the choice that makes the need clear enough to plan, build, and test.
assessment_bank.option_a: Add the exact request to the Sprint without clarification
assessment_bank.option_b: Turn the need into a clear backlog item or user story with testable acceptance criteria
assessment_bank.option_c: Ask the Scrum Master to choose the technical solution
assessment_bank.option_d: Wait until the Sprint Review to define the need

assessment_bank.prompt: Which Scrum event focuses on improving how the team works?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The Sprint Retrospective supports improvements to quality and effectiveness.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Separate product feedback from process improvement.
assessment_bank.option_a: Sprint Planning
assessment_bank.option_b: Sprint Review
assessment_bank.option_c: Sprint Retrospective
assessment_bank.option_d: Daily Scrum

assessment_bank.prompt: Which user story is strongest?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The story identifies a user, a goal, and a benefit.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Look for who needs what and why it matters.
assessment_bank.option_a: Add reminders to Student Hub
assessment_bank.option_b: As a developer, I want to use a database
assessment_bank.option_c: The system shall send messages
assessment_bank.option_d: As a student, I want assignment reminders so that I can plan my work

assessment_bank.prompt: Which acceptance criterion is testable?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The criterion describes an observable product result.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Choose the statement that a tester can verify.
assessment_bank.option_a: The reminder page should look modern
assessment_bank.option_b: A keyboard user can set and cancel a reminder
assessment_bank.option_c: Students will probably like reminders
assessment_bank.option_d: The feature should work well

assessment_bank.prompt: A team has less capacity than expected. Which Sprint plan is strongest?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The plan connects value, capacity, and a shared Sprint Goal.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Protect focus and quality while selecting achievable work.
assessment_bank.option_a: Select every high priority item
assessment_bank.option_b: Lower the quality standard
assessment_bank.option_c: Choose work that supports one Sprint Goal and fits capacity
assessment_bank.option_d: Let each person choose unrelated work

assessment_bank.prompt: What should the Scrum Team establish during Sprint Planning?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Sprint Planning addresses value, selected work, and an initial plan.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Think about the three topics in Sprint Planning.
assessment_bank.option_a: Why the Sprint is valuable, what can be done, and how the work will be completed
assessment_bank.option_b: A fixed task assignment that cannot change
assessment_bank.option_c: A release promise for the entire Product Backlog
assessment_bank.option_d: A list of stakeholder complaints without priorities

assessment_bank.prompt: Developers disagree about how to build a feature. What is the best Agile response?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Developers collaborate and manage how they complete their work.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Preserve shared responsibility and team self management.
assessment_bank.option_a: Ask the Scrum Master to act as their boss
assessment_bank.option_b: Let the Product Owner assign each technical task
assessment_bank.option_c: Allow one developer to decide without discussion
assessment_bank.option_d: Discuss evidence and let the self managing Developers choose a plan

assessment_bank.prompt: A blocker threatens the Sprint Goal. What should a team member do?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Clear communication helps the team inspect progress and adapt.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Choose the response that supports transparency and shared action.
assessment_bank.option_a: Hide it until the Sprint ends
assessment_bank.option_b: Make it visible and work with the team to address it
assessment_bank.option_c: Complete unrelated work without telling the team
assessment_bank.option_d: Lower the Definition of Done

assessment_bank.prompt: Users report that course filters would make Student Hub more useful. What should happen next?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Review feedback can guide future Product Backlog decisions.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Feedback informs what the product should do next.
assessment_bank.option_a: Use the feedback to reconsider Product Backlog order
assessment_bank.option_b: Add the feature without checking value or effort
assessment_bank.option_c: Replace the Sprint Goal during the review
assessment_bank.option_d: Ignore the feedback because the Increment works

assessment_bank.prompt: What is the main purpose of a Sprint Review?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The Sprint Review connects a working result with stakeholder evidence.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Focus on the product outcome and future decisions.
assessment_bank.option_a: Assign blame for unfinished tasks
assessment_bank.option_b: Approve individual employee performance
assessment_bank.option_c: Prevent changes to the Product Backlog
assessment_bank.option_d: Inspect the Sprint outcome with stakeholders and discuss adaptations

assessment_bank.prompt: Which retrospective improvement is most actionable?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. The improvement is specific and can be tested during the next Sprint.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Choose a process change with a clear action and time.
assessment_bank.option_a: Communicate better
assessment_bank.option_b: Avoid all future blockers
assessment_bank.option_c: Test keyboard access before merging each backlog item next Sprint
assessment_bank.option_d: Work harder when problems appear

assessment_bank.prompt: A team missed several blockers until late in the Sprint. Which evidence should guide its retrospective?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. A retrospective uses process evidence to improve team effectiveness.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Select evidence about how the team worked.
assessment_bank.option_a: Which product features stakeholders want next
assessment_bank.option_b: When blockers appeared and how the team communicated them
assessment_bank.option_c: Which person completed the most tasks
assessment_bank.option_d: How many items remain in the full Product Backlog

assessment_bank.prompt: What is the main value of a Scrum or Kanban style board?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. A board helps the team see and discuss the state of work.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Choose the tool benefit related to transparency.
assessment_bank.option_a: It automatically assigns tasks
assessment_bank.option_b: It replaces the Product Backlog
assessment_bank.option_c: It makes work status and flow visible
assessment_bank.option_d: It prevents the plan from changing

assessment_bank.prompt: A backlog item becomes urgent after new user evidence appears. What should the team do?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Agile project tools support visible, evidence based changes.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Use the tool to represent the team's current decision.
assessment_bank.option_a: Keep the old order because it was approved
assessment_bank.option_b: Start every item at once
assessment_bank.option_c: Delete lower items without discussion
assessment_bank.option_d: Make the evidence visible and reconsider the backlog order

assessment_bank.prompt: When can completed work become part of an Increment?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Work must meet the Definition of Done to become part of an Increment.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Look for the shared quality standard.
assessment_bank.option_a: When coding begins
assessment_bank.option_b: When it meets the Definition of Done
assessment_bank.option_c: When the Sprint Goal is written
assessment_bank.option_d: When a stakeholder first requests it

assessment_bank.prompt: A reminder feature sends alerts, but users cannot cancel them as required. What is the correct conclusion?
assessment_bank.feedback_correct: Correct. Functional software must satisfy its defined acceptance criteria.
assessment_bank.feedback_incorrect: Compare the tested result with every required outcome.
assessment_bank.option_a: The feature does not yet meet its acceptance criteria
assessment_bank.option_b: The feature is complete because it sends alerts
assessment_bank.option_c: The Product Goal must be canceled
assessment_bank.option_d: The Sprint Review should be skipped
